nodes.label: Spec-Driven Development (SDD)
nodes.rationale: Addresses reliability debt and mental model loss from vibe coding. Puts specification (explicit external behavior: inputs/outputs, invariants, preconditions, postconditions, acceptance criteria) at the center rather than code. Idea: 'intent is the source of truth' rather than 'code is the source of truth'. Separates design from implementation and enables AI agents to stop guessing and start executing. Improves incident debuggability, onboarding, and spec serves as reviewable contract.

nodes.label: Context Engineering for AI Agents
nodes.rationale: Deliberately curating what information AI agents have access to during long-horizon tasks. A well-written spec.md IS context engineering. Windsurfrules and AGENTS.md encode persistent project context. Kiro steering files support inclusion modes for granular agent context control.

nodes.label: REST API Architectural Style
nodes.rationale: REST (Representational State Transfer) is a stateless, client-server, cacheable, layered architectural style for distributed systems. Resource model is the central concept. URI design rules, HTTP method semantics, and status code conventions are the building blocks of well-designed RESTful APIs. References Roy Fielding's dissertation.

nodes.label: Docs as Code Principle
nodes.rationale: Documentation stored in version control (Git), built automatically as artifacts, published without human intervention. Solves: docs not part of codebase/CI-CD, not reviewed, written in separate tools. Enables collaboration, versioning, and tracking docs as bugs. Toolchain: static site generators (Docusaurus, Hugo, Gatsby), diagram-as-code (Mermaid, PlantUML), source-code doc generators (Sphinx).

nodes.label: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
nodes.rationale: Open protocol by Anthropic that standardizes how AI applications interact with external systems via Tools, Resources, and Prompts. Transforms N×M integration problem into N+M. Analogous to what APIs did for web apps or LSP for code editors. Enables centralized auth via OAuth 2.0, consistent audit trails, team specialization, and vendor flexibility. Future: remote servers via SSE+OAuth2, MCP registries, .well-known endpoints.

nodes.label: MongoDB Sharded Cluster Architecture
nodes.rationale: Sharding splits data across nodes (horizontal partitioning) as opposed to replica sets which keep identical data on multiple servers. Components: mongos (query router), config servers (metadata about chunk locations, must be a replica set), and shard replica sets. Auto-sharding balances data automatically. Config servers must come up first and be backed up.

nodes.label: OAuth 2.0 Protocol
nodes.rationale: Industry-standard authorization protocol enabling delegated access without credential sharing. Core roles: Resource Owner, Client, Authorization Server, Resource Server. Four grant types: Authorization Code (most secure, server-side), Implicit (deprecated), Resource Owner Password (avoid), Client Credentials (service-to-service). PKCE enhances security for public clients. Tokens: short-lived access tokens + long-lived refresh tokens. Extension: OIDC adds authentication on top.

nodes.label: Kerberos Protocol
nodes.rationale: Network authentication protocol using secret-key cryptography, developed at MIT in the 1980s. Passwords never sent over network; uses time-limited tickets for SSO. Trade-off: strong security but requires clock synchronization, complex setup, and KDC as single point of failure.

nodes.label: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
nodes.rationale: Modern authentication protocol built on OAuth 2.0. Best for web and mobile applications. Uses JSON/JWT format over HTTPS. Provides SSO and federated identity. Trade-off: excellent mobile/SPA support and developer experience but lacks native PostgreSQL support.

nodes.label: LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol)
nodes.rationale: Open, vendor-neutral directory service protocol for accessing hierarchical user/system information. Not an authentication protocol itself but commonly used for authentication. Trade-off: centralized user management and scalability, but complex setup, potential cleartext passwords in default config, and management overhead.

nodes.label: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language)
nodes.rationale: XML-based open standard for exchanging authentication/authorization data, developed by OASIS. SAML 2.0 released 2005. Cornerstone of enterprise SSO. Trade-off: enterprise maturity and rich access control, but XML complexity, large message size, poor mobile support, and implementation difficulty.

nodes.label: OAuth 2.0
nodes.rationale: Primarily an authorization protocol (delegated access), not authentication. Foundation for OIDC. Uses JSON over HTTPS. Trade-off: excellent for API authorization and third-party integration, but limited for direct user authentication and enterprise SSO.

nodes.label: Spec-Driven Development (SDD)
nodes.rationale: SDD inverts the power structure: specs don't serve code, code serves specs. Spec is the source of truth, written first. AI generates code from specs. Debugging means fixing the spec. Trade-offs: powerful for 3-8 point features and greenfield, but 'sledgehammer for a nut' on small bug fixes, can create false sense of control, and reviewing markdown is harder than reviewing code.

nodes.label: spec-kit
nodes.rationale: GitHub's open-source SDD toolkit distributed as a CLI. Three commands: init, specify, plan, tasks. All artifacts live in .specify/ folder, versioned alongside code. Reduces ~12 hours of documentation to ~15 minutes. Works with Windsurf, Cursor, Claude, GitHub Copilot.

nodes.label: Three Levels of SDD
nodes.rationale: Level 1 Spec-First: write spec to focus AI for this feature, may discard. Level 2 Spec-Anchored: keep and evolve spec with feature (spec-kit targets this). Level 3 Spec-as-Source: spec IS primary artifact, code is generated output. Most teams start at Level 1.

nodes.label: SDD Tradeoffs and When to Use
nodes.rationale: SDD is not a silver bullet. Per Martin Fowler: 'Sledgehammer for a nut' for small bugs, 'False sense of control' since AI doesn't always follow instructions, 'Reviewing markdown harder than code'. Use for 3-8 point features and greenfield. Skip for small bugs and emergency hotfixes. Start Level 1, earn Level 2.

nodes.label: Spec-Driven Development (SDD)
nodes.rationale: SDD inverts traditional development: specs serve as the source of truth instead of code. Three levels exist: Spec-First (disposable), Spec-Anchored (lives alongside code), and Spec-as-Source (code is generated output). Motivation: AI can now reliably translate natural language specs to code, complexity is exponential, and pivots are normal — regenerating from spec beats manual rewrites.

nodes.label: spec-kit CLI Toolkit
nodes.rationale: GitHub's open-source SDD toolkit. Targets Level 2 (Spec-Anchored). All artifacts live in repo under .specify/ folder, versioned with code. Works with Windsurf, Cursor, Claude, GitHub Copilot.

nodes.label: SDD Constitution (Immutable AI Principles)
nodes.rationale: The constitution is a memory/constitution.md file defining immutable principles applied to every AI interaction. Nine articles cover: Library-First, CLI Interface, Test-First, Integration tests, Research-driven, Versioning, Simplicity Gate, Anti-Abstraction, Integration-First. Equivalent to Windsurf .windsurfrules.

nodes.label: Vibe Coding (Code-First AI Development)
nodes.rationale: Contrasted with SDD: unstructured prompts lead to AI guessing and architectural drift. Failure mode is silent drift vs SDD's visible test failures.

nodes.label: Telos Method (Purpose Framework)
nodes.rationale: Framework by Daniel Miessler for achieving clarity in the AI age. A Telos File is a personal operating manual capturing purpose, challenges, history, and goals — enabling self-clarity and rich AI context. Core insight: human value is shifting from task execution to problem definition.

nodes.label: Pass Unix Password Manager
nodes.rationale: Follows Unix philosophy: stores passwords as GPG-encrypted files in a directory structure, integrates with Git for sync. Chosen for simplicity, transparency, GPG industry-standard encryption, and CLI-first design.

nodes.label: Go Goroutines and Concurrency
nodes.rationale: Goroutines enable concurrent execution of functions. Used with worker pools and semaphores to check 3000+ SQL servers simultaneously with bounded parallelism.

nodes.rationale: Low commitment entry point: write a spec before each task, may be discarded after. Recommended starting point for most teams before graduating to Spec-Anchored.

nodes.label: Spec-Anchored Level
nodes.rationale: Medium commitment: spec lives alongside code forever and evolves with the feature. Requires team alignment.

nodes.label: Spec-as-Source Level
nodes.rationale: High commitment: spec is the primary artifact and code is generated output. Requires strong tooling.
